title: GitLab tokens, visibility and audit streaming
volume: Tokens: a few a week where developers make their own. Projects made public and streaming changes are rare.
mdr_note: These detections are yours to work. Sophos MDR doesn't work custom detections, and a case your own case rule opens from them is Managed By Self.
author: Aaronjacobs000
summary: Three custom detection rules for GitLab, on the CloudAudit records the library's GitLab parsers write from streamed audit events. They make a detection when someone creates an access token, makes a project public, or changes audit event streaming. Each rule matches sensor type GitLab only.
notes:
Setup:
- Add the library's GitLab parsers, and point a GitLab audit event streaming destination at HTTP Ingest, as the parser entry says. Then run the check-your-data search to see events arrive.

How it works:
- The parsers write GitLab's event type, such as personal_access_token_created, as the event name and the author as the user.
- The visibility rule takes project_visibility_level_updated whose new value is Public. GitLab writes the change's from and to values, which the parsers keep in request_parameters.
- The streaming rule takes every audit_events_streaming event type, for an instance or a group.

Tuning:
- If a service account creates project tokens for CI, leave it out of the token rule in the query itself, such as and user_name != 'ci-bot'. A suppression rule would hide Sophos's detections for that account as well.

Testing:
- In a lab tenant on 2026-11-23, each query returned exactly the sample lines tests.json lists in Data Lake Search, and the rules run offline on the same 5 records agreed. The samples went in with their dates moved to the day before the test, so they fell inside the search's time range.
- As live rules there, each one fired on exactly its sample lines within about a minute. The lines went in 24 minutes after the rules were made, and every rule fired on the first send.
- No Sophos detector made a detection on the lines these rules take. Sophos's sign-in analytics flagged only a sample sign-in on Auth, as an unseen user, address or application.
- The events went to HTTP Ingest one per request as JSON, as GitLab's streaming destination sends them.

Known gaps:
- The parsers write the author's display name as the user, so two people with the same name share a case.
- A group made public (group_visibility_level_updated) isn't taken.
